title: Revisiting Smoothed Online Learning:Competitive Ratio, Dynamic Regret with Switching Cost, and Best of Both Worlds

paper.title: Revisiting Smoothed Online Learning: Competitive Ratio, Dynamic Regret with Switching Cost, and Best of Both Worlds
paper.abstract:
Abstract We revisit smoothed online learning and develop algorithms with improved competitive ratios, optimal dynamic regret
with switching cost, and best-of-both-worlds guarantees. Surprisingly, minimizing the hitting cost alone is max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}) -competitive for α \alpha -polyhedral functions under the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm
switching cost and 1 + 4 λ 1+\frac{4}{\lambda} -competitive for λ \lambda -quadratic growth functions under the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, significantly improving existing guarantees.
The polyhedral bound is tight for this naive algorithm, and we establish a matching lower bound for α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 .
For convex λ \lambda -quadratic growth hitting costs, minimizing a suitably weighted sum of hitting and squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching costs yields a competitive ratio of 1 + 2 λ 1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}} .
For dynamic regret with the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, we develop Smoothed Ader (SAder), which achieves the
optimal O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) rate in the standard online convex optimization setting, where P T P_{T} is the
comparator’s path-length. Its lookahead version removes the bounded-gradient assumption, and a matching lower bound establishes
optimality in this setting. Finally, for convex hitting costs on a bounded convex domain, we develop UDNP to aggregate any two experts in the lookahead setting under both switching costs. Its additional cumulative cost is at most O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) relative to the first expert and O ⁡ ( T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(\sqrt{T\log T}) relative to the second, yielding best-of-both-worlds guarantees without bounded gradients.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Online learning is the process of making a sequence of predictions given knowledge of the answers to previous tasks and possibly additional information ( Shalev-Shwartz, 2011 ) . While traditional online learning aims to make the prediction as accurate as possible, in this paper, we study smoothed online learning (SOL), where the online learner incurs a switching cost for changing its predictions between rounds ( Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2013 ) . SOL has received considerable attention recently because in many real-world applications, a change of action usually brings some additional cost. Examples include the dynamic right-sizing for data centers ( Lin et al., 2011 ) , geographical load balancing ( Lin et al., 2012 ) , real-time electricity pricing ( Kim and Giannakis, 2014 ) , video streaming ( Joseph and de Veciana, 2012 ) , spatiotemporal sequence prediction ( Kim et al., 2015 ) , multi-timescale control ( Goel et al., 2017 ) , and thermal management ( Zanini et al., 2010 ) . Specifically, SOL is performed in a sequence of consecutive rounds, where at round t t the learner is asked to select a point 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} from the decision set 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , and suffers a hitting cost f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) . Depending on the performance metric, the learner may be allowed to observe f t ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{t}(\cdot) when making decisions, which is different from the traditional online learning in which f t ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{t}(\cdot) is revealed only after the learner submits its decision ( Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2006 ) . Additionally, the learner also incurs a switching cost m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1}) for changing decisions between successive rounds. Common choices for the switching cost include the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm distance ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ \|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\| and the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ 2 / 2 \|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\|^{2}/2 ( Goel et al., 2019 ) . In the literature, there are two performance metrics for SOL: competitive ratio and dynamic regret with switching cost. Competitive ratio is popular in the community of online algorithms ( Borodin and El-Yaniv, 1998 ) . It is defined as the worst-case ratio of the total cost incurred by the online learner to the offline optimal cost: ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) ) min ⁡ ∑ t = 1 T 𝐮 0 , 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ ( f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) + m ⁡ ( 𝐮 t , 𝐮 t − 1 ) ) . \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1})\big)}{\min_{\mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})+m(\mathbf{u}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t-1})\big)}. (1) When focusing on the competitive ratio, we consider the lookahead setting, in which the learner observes f t ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{t}(\cdot) before picking 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} . The problem is still nontrivial due to the coupling created by the switching cost. Dynamic regret with switching cost extends dynamic regret ( Zinkevich, 2003 ) by accounting for switching costs. Whereas competitive ratio measures a multiplicative comparison with the offline optimum, dynamic regret measures the additive difference between the learner’s total cost and that of an arbitrary comparator sequence 𝐮 0 , 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X} : ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) ) − ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) + m ⁡ ( 𝐮 t , 𝐮 t − 1 ) ) . \sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1})\big)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})+m(\mathbf{u}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t-1})\big). (2) We keep the comparator sequence explicit in ( 2 ), rather than minimizing over it as in previous work ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Goel et al., 2019 ) , and seek bounds that adapt to its regularity, measured by the path-length P T = ∑ t = 1 T ‖ 𝐮 t − 𝐮 t − 1 ‖ . P_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\mathbf{u}_{t}-\mathbf{u}_{t-1}\|. (3) For dynamic regret with switching cost, we consider both the standard OCO setting and the lookahead setting.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: Online balanced descent (OBD) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) balances the hitting and switching costs by projecting the previous decision onto a suitably chosen sublevel set of the current hitting-cost function. OBD and its variants ( Goel et al., 2019 ) exploit structural properties of the hitting costs to obtain dimension-free competitive ratios. These results motivate examining the simpler greedy algorithm, which selects its decision by solving min 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 f t ​ ( 𝐱 ) + γ ​ m ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐱 t − 1 ) , \min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\quad f_{t}(\mathbf{x})+\gamma m(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{t-1}), (4) where γ ≥ 0 \gamma\geq 0 is a trade-off parameter. As a special case of Regularized OBD (R-OBD), a suitably tuned greedy algorithm achieves the optimal competitive ratio for strongly convex hitting costs under the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost ( Goel et al., 2019 ) . Moreover, Lin et al. (2020) analyze the choice γ = 0 \gamma=0 , referred to as the naive approach, for polyhedral and quadratic growth functions. We revisit these simple algorithms to sharpen their competitive guarantees under different growth conditions and to clarify when explicitly accounting for switching costs improves performance. For dynamic regret, neither the guarantee of OBD nor that of R-OBD provides an adaptive bound for the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost. OBD requires a prescribed upper bound on the comparator’s path-length, and its regret bound depends on this upper bound rather than the actual path-length ( Chen et al., 2018 , Corollary 11) . R-OBD provides an adaptive guarantee, but for the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost ( Goel et al., 2019 ) . Moreover, both guarantees require lookahead access to the current hitting cost. We therefore seek adaptive dynamic-regret guarantees for the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost under both standard and lookahead feedback. We also investigate whether a single algorithm can achieve both a competitive-ratio guarantee and an adaptive dynamic-regret guarantee, connecting to earlier work on combining the two criteria ( Andrew et al., 2013 ; Daniely and Mansour, 2019 ) . Expert aggregation offers a natural approach, but directly applying this approach requires a known bound on the experts’ one-round cost differences. We investigate how lookahead information can overcome this obstacle without imposing an additional bounded-gradient assumption. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

sections.heading: Competitive Ratio
sections.text: We sharpen the competitive guarantees of the naive and greedy algorithms and establish complementary lower bounds. For α \alpha -polyhedral hitting costs and the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, the naive algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max\left(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}\right) . This improves upon the 3 + 8 α 3+\frac{8}{\alpha} ratio of OBD ( Chen et al., 2018 ) and the 1 + 2 α 1+\frac{2}{\alpha} bound of Lin et al. (2020, Lemma 1) . We show that this bound is tight for the naive algorithm and cannot be improved by any fixed choice of γ \gamma in the greedy algorithm. Moreover, we establish a matching lower bound for α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 . For λ \lambda -quadratic growth hitting costs and the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, the naive algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of 1 + 4 λ 1+\frac{4}{\lambda} , improving upon the max ⁡ ( 1 + 6 λ , 4 ) \max\left(1+\frac{6}{\lambda},4\right) bound of Lin et al. (2020, Lemma 1) and matching, as λ \lambda tends to zero, the order of the lower bound for this algorithm in Goel et al. (2019, Theorem 5) . Neither this guarantee nor the polyhedral guarantee requires convexity. Under additional convexity, a suitable choice of γ > 0 \gamma>0 yields a competitive ratio of 1 + 2 λ 1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}} , improving the naive guarantee for small λ \lambda . Compared with Greedy OBD ( Goel et al., 2019 , Theorem 3) , our guarantee has the same asymptotic order with much smaller constants, although it requires convexity rather than quasiconvexity. Our analysis of the naive and greedy algorithms is also simpler, avoiding the geometric arguments used for OBD and Greedy OBD.

sections.heading: Dynamic Regret with Switching Cost
sections.text: For convex hitting costs and the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, we develop Smoothed Ader (SAder) by extending Ader ( Zhang et al., 2018a ) , an algorithm that achieves optimal dynamic regret in standard online convex optimization. Ader uses Hedge ( Freund and Schapire, 1997 ) to aggregate online gradient descent (OGD) experts ( Zinkevich, 2003 ) with different step sizes. SAder modifies this approach by incorporating the experts’ switching costs into the meta-algorithm’s losses. Under the standard bounded-domain and bounded-gradient assumptions, SAder achieves an optimal O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) bound on the sum of dynamic regret and the learner’s switching cost, matching Ader’s rate despite the additional switching cost. Compared with OBD ( Chen et al., 2018 , Corollary 11) , SAder adapts to the actual path-length P T P_{T} without requiring a prescribed upper bound on P T P_{T} or lookahead feedback. We further develop lookahead SAder, whose greedy experts generate predictions using the current hitting cost. The meta-algorithm updates the aggregation weights using the experts’ current one-round costs before making its decision. Lookahead SAder achieves the same O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) regret bound without assuming bounded gradients. We establish a matching Ω ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) \Omega(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) lower bound in the lookahead setting, showing that this rate is optimal up to constant factors.

sections.heading: Best of Both Worlds
sections.text: We develop UDNP, an unbounded-input variant of the Discounted-Normal-Predictor ( Kapralov and Panigrahy, 2011 ) , to aggregate any two experts in the lookahead setting. Building on expert aggregation with switching costs ( Daniely and Mansour, 2019 ) , UDNP exploits lookahead information to handle potentially unbounded differences between the experts’ one-round costs, without requiring a prescribed bound on these differences or a bounded-gradient assumption. Our approach applies to both the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm and squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching costs. For convex hitting costs on a bounded convex domain, the learner’s total cost exceeds that of the first expert by at most a constant and that of the second expert by at most O ⁡ ( T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(\sqrt{T\log T}) . Thus, when the first expert provides a competitive-ratio guarantee and the second a dynamic-regret guarantee, UDNP preserves the former up to an additive constant while adding only an O ⁡ ( T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(\sqrt{T\log T}) term to the latter. As concrete applications, we instantiate this approach with experts analyzed in this paper. For convex hitting costs satisfying the α \alpha -polyhedral condition, combining the naive algorithm with lookahead SAder under the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost yields the competitive factor max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max\left(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}\right) up to an additive constant and an O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) + T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}+\sqrt{T\log T}) dynamic-regret bound. For convex hitting costs satisfying the λ \lambda -quadratic growth condition, combining two greedy experts under the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost yields the competitive factor 1 + 2 λ 1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}} up to an additive constant and an O ⁡ ( P T + T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(P_{T}+\sqrt{T\log T}) dynamic-regret bound.

sections.heading: Extensions over the Conference Version
sections.text: A preliminary version of this paper was presented at the 35th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) . The present paper extends that version in the following aspects: • We extend the competitive-ratio analysis for polyhedral hitting costs. We prove that the max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max\left(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}\right) bound from the conference version is tight for the naive algorithm and cannot be improved by any fixed choice of γ \gamma in the greedy algorithm. We further establish a matching lower bound for α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 . • We develop UDNP to address the best-of-both-worlds question left open in the conference version. For the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, we establish general guarantees for aggregating arbitrary pairs of experts while handling potentially unbounded cost differences without assuming bounded gradients. We instantiate these guarantees by combining the naive algorithm with lookahead SAder. • We extend UDNP to the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost through a new interpolation inequality. The resulting aggregation guarantee also applies to arbitrary pairs of experts, and we instantiate it with two greedy experts. We further establish a dynamic-regret bound for the greedy algorithm under general convexity, allowing nonsmooth hitting costs and constrained minimizers. • We revise lookahead SAder to update its aggregation weights using the experts’ current one-round costs, removing the circular dependence on the current meta-decision. We also provide a proof based on the strong convexity of the experts’ regularized objectives, without requiring differentiability of the hitting costs.

sections.heading: Organization
sections.text: We review related work in Section 2 and study the competitive ratios of the naive and greedy algorithms in Section 3 . Section 4 develops SAder and its lookahead variant for dynamic regret with switching cost. The best-of-both-worlds framework, UDNP, is presented in Section 5 for both the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm and squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching costs. Proofs of the main results appear in Section 6 , with proofs of supporting lemmas deferred to the appendices. We conclude the paper and discuss future directions in Section 7 .

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: This section reviews related work on smoothed online learning (SOL), dynamic regret, and online optimization with switching constraints.

sections.heading: 2.1 Smoothed Online Learning
sections.text: SOL has been investigated under the setting of multi-armed bandits ( Agrawal et al., 1990 ; Guha and Munagala, 2009 ; Dekel et al., 2014 ; Koren et al., 2017a ; Koren et al., 2017b ) , prediction with expert advice ( Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2013 ) , and online convex optimization ( Lin et al., 2011 ; Bansal et al., 2015 ; Zhao et al., 2020b ) . In the following, we mainly discuss smoothed online convex optimization (SOCO). The early works on SOCO are motivated by real-world applications with switching costs, and focus on designing competitive algorithms in the low-dimensional setting ( Lin et al., 2011 ) . In particular, Bansal et al. (2015) show that for SOCO on the real line, the competitive ratio can be upper bounded by 2 2 , which is proved to be optimal ( Antoniadis and Schewior, 2018 ) . They also establish a competitive ratio of 3 3 under the memoryless setting. In the study of SOCO, it is common to assume that the learner has access to predictions of future hitting costs, and several algorithms ( Lin et al., 2012 ; Chen et al., 2015 ; Chen et al., 2016 ; Li et al., 2018 ; Li and Li, 2020 ) have been developed based on receding horizon control (RHC) ( Kwon and Han, 2005 ) . In fact, the greedy algorithm in ( 4 ) can be treated as a variant of RHC. However, previous results for RHC are limited to special problems, and ( 4 ) remains under-explored. For example, with a prediction window of length W W , Li et al. (2018) derive a dynamic-regret bound with switching cost that decreases exponentially with W W , under assumptions including strong convexity and smoothness. One milestone is the online balanced descent (OBD) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) , which has a dimension-free competitive ratio even when the learner can only observe the hitting cost of the current round. Specifically, OBD iteratively projects the previous point onto a carefully chosen level set of the hitting cost so as to balance the switching cost and the hitting cost. When the hitting cost is α \alpha -polyhedral and convex, and the switching cost is the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm distance, OBD attains a 3 + 8 α 3+\frac{8}{\alpha} competitive ratio. Furthermore, OBD can also be tuned to control the dynamic regret with switching cost. Let L L be an upper bound of the path-length of the comparator sequence, i.e., P T ≤ L P_{T}\leq L . Chen et al. (2018, Corollary 11) have proved that ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ ) − min ⁡ ∑ t = 1 T P T ≤ L ⁡ ( f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) + ‖ 𝐮 t − 𝐮 t − 1 ‖ ) = O ⁡ ( T ​ L ) \sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\|\big)-\min_{P_{T}\leq L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})+\|\mathbf{u}_{t}-\mathbf{u}_{t-1}\|\big)=O\left(\sqrt{TL}\right) (5) leading to sublinear regret when L = o ⁡ ( T ) L=o(T) . However, there are two limitations: (i) the value of L L needs to be given as a parameter; and (ii) it is nonadaptive because the upper bound depends on L L instead of the actual path-length P T P_{T} . R-OBD includes ( 4 ) as a special case, which also enjoys the optimal competitive ratio for strongly convex functions. Furthermore, Goel et al. (2019, Theorem 6) analyze the dynamic regret of R-OBD, and the following bound can be extracted from their proof by setting λ 1 = 1 \lambda_{1}=1 and λ 2 = 0 \lambda_{2}=0 : ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ 2 ) − ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) + 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐮 t − 𝐮 t − 1 ‖ 2 ) = O ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) . \sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\|^{2}\right)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{t}-\mathbf{u}_{t-1}\|^{2}\right)=O(1+P_{T}). Compared with ( 5 ), this bound is adaptive because it depends on the actual path-length of the comparator sequence. However, this squared-norm guarantee does not cover the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost. Moreover, the proof uses a vanishing gradient condition for the regularized objective, which need not hold at a constrained minimizer. When the hitting cost is both quasiconvex and λ \lambda -quadratic growth, Goel et al. (2019, Theorem 3) have demonstrated that their Greedy OBD algorithm attains an O ⁡ ( 1 / λ ) O(1/\sqrt{\lambda}) competitive ratio, as λ → 0 \lambda\rightarrow 0 . Lin et al. (2020) have analyzed the naive approach which ignores the switching cost and simply minimizes the hitting cost in each round, i.e., the greedy algorithm with γ = 0 \gamma=0 . It is a bit surprising that this naive approach is 1 + 2 α 1+\frac{2}{\alpha} -competitive for α \alpha -polyhedral functions and max ⁡ ( 1 + 6 λ , 4 ) \max(1+\frac{6}{\lambda},4) -competitive for λ \lambda -quadratic growth functions, without any convexity assumption ( Lin et al., 2020 , Lemma 1) . Argue et al. (2020a) have investigated a hybrid setting in which the hitting cost is both λ \lambda -strongly convex and H H -smooth, but the switching cost is the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm instead of the squared one. They develop Constrained OBD, and establish a 4 + 4 ​ 2 ​ H / λ 4+4\sqrt{2H/\lambda} competitive ratio. However, their analysis requires the hitting costs to be globally nonnegative, rather than merely nonnegative on the feasible set 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . To facilitate comparisons, we summarize the competitive ratios of OBD, its variants, and the greedy algorithm in Table 1 . SOCO is closely related to convex body chasing (CBC), where the learner selects a point from each arriving convex body and seeks to minimize the total movement ( Friedman and Linial, 1993 ; Antoniadis et al., 2016 ; Bansal et al., 2018 ; Argue et al., 2019 ; Bubeck et al., 2019 ; Bubeck et al., 2020 ) . For general CBC in Euclidean space, algorithms achieve a competitive ratio of O ⁡ ( min ⁡ { d , d ​ log ⁡ T } ) O(\min\{d,\sqrt{d\log T}\}) ( Argue et al., 2020b ; Sellke, 2020 ) , while a lower bound of Ω ⁡ ( d ) \Omega(\sqrt{d}) is known ( Friedman and Linial, 1993 ) . Recent work investigates how to incorporate advice into competitive algorithms for SOCO and related chasing problems while retaining worst-case guarantees. Christianson et al. (2022) combine black-box advice with a competitive algorithm for convex body and function chasing; for polyhedral hitting costs, they use the naive approach from our conference version ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) as the competitive baseline. For possibly nonconvex α \alpha -polyhedral hitting costs, Rutten et al. (2023) establish near-optimal tradeoffs between consistency and robustness with untrusted predictions. Christianson et al. (2023) further characterize such tradeoffs in the more general framework of metrical task systems. Recent work also develops dynamic-regret guarantees for SOCO in several directions. Zhang et al. (2022) obtain interval-wise regret guarantees using Discounted-Normal-Predictor ( Kapralov and Panigrahy, 2011 ) , while Yang et al. (2025) consider delayed gradient feedback. Mhaisen and Iosifidis (2026) introduce partially lazy gradient updates and aggregate the resulting experts using the SAder meta-algorithm from our conference version ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) , retaining the optimal O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) dynamic regret with switching cost. Alongside these dynamic-regret results, Bhuyan et al. (2024) seek simultaneous guarantees in adversarial and stochastic environments. For quadratic hitting costs and squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching costs, they combine adversarial competitiveness with near-optimal stochastic performance when the hitting-cost minimizers form a martingale whose increments have a common covariance matrix. Our focus is on simultaneously controlling the competitive ratio and dynamic regret against arbitrary comparator sequences in the lookahead setting. sections.heading: 2.2 Dynamic Regret
sections.text: Recently, dynamic regret has attracted considerable interest in the community of online learning ( Zhang, 2020 ) . The motivation of dynamic regret is to deal with changing environments, in which the optimal decision may change over time. It is defined as the difference between the cumulative loss of the learner and that of a sequence of comparators 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X} : D-Regret ( 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ) = ∑ t = 1 T f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) − ∑ t = 1 T f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) . \DReg(\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t}). (6) In the general form of dynamic regret, 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T \mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T} could be an arbitrary sequence ( Zinkevich, 2003 ; Hall and Willett, 2013 ; Zhang et al., 2018a ; Zhang et al., 2020 ; Cutkosky, 2020 ; Zhao et al., 2020a ; Baby and Wang, 2021 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . In the restricted form, the comparators are chosen as per-round minimizers, i.e., 𝐮 t ∈ argmin 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 f t ​ ( 𝐱 ) \mathbf{u}_{t}\in\argmin_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}f_{t}(\mathbf{x}) ( Jadbabaie et al., 2015 ; Besbes et al., 2015 ; Yang et al., 2016 ; Mokhtari et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ; Zhang et al., 2018b ; Wan et al., 2021 ; Zhao and Zhang, 2021 ; Xu and Zhang, 2024 ) . While it is well-known that sublinear dynamic regret is unattainable in the worst case, one can bound the dynamic regret in terms of some regularities of the comparator sequence. An instance is given by Zinkevich (2003) , who introduces the notion of path-length defined in ( 3 ) to measure the temporal variability of the comparator sequence, and derives an O ​ ( T ​ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T}(1+P_{T})) bound for the dynamic regret of OGD. Later, Zhang et al. (2018a) develop adaptive learning for dynamic environment (Ader), which achieves the optimal O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) dynamic regret. In this paper, we show that a small change of Ader attains the same bound for dynamic regret with switching cost. We summarize our results and representative previous guarantees in Table 2 .

sections.heading: 2.3 Switching Constraints
sections.text: Another line of work studies online convex optimization under explicit switching constraints. Chen et al. (2020) characterize the minimax regret when the learner is allowed only a limited number of switches. Sherman and Koren (2023) study a related formulation in which the switching budget is imposed in expectation. Subsequent work improves regret guarantees under this expected switch-count budget ( Agarwal et al., 2023 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , with Agarwal et al. (2024) obtaining better dimension dependence without requiring smooth losses. Beyond switch-count constraints, Wang et al. (2021) impose a budget on the cumulative movement of the learner and establish minimax-optimal regret bounds for convex losses. This formulation accounts for the distance between consecutive decisions, allowing finer control over movement than counting each change equally. These studies minimize hitting-cost regret against the best fixed decision while satisfying a prescribed switching budget. In our setting, switching costs are included in the objective together with hitting costs, so the learner directly trades off the two types of costs.

sections.heading: 3 Competitive Ratio
sections.text: In this section, we study competitive ratio as the performance metric. Throughout the paper, we assume nonnegative hitting costs whenever competitive ratio is considered, as in prior work ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Argue et al., 2020a ) . For our competitive-ratio guarantees, the minimization in ( 1 ) is restricted to comparator sequences with 𝐮 0 = 𝐱 0 \mathbf{u}_{0}=\mathbf{x}_{0} .

sections.heading: 3.1 Polyhedral Functions
sections.text: We first introduce the definition of polyhedral functions. Definition 1 . A function f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) : 𝒳 → ℝ f(\cdot):\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} with minimizer 𝐯 \mathbf{v} is α \alpha -polyhedral if f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) − f ⁡ ( 𝐯 ) ≥ α ​ ‖ 𝐱 − 𝐯 ‖ , ∀ 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 . f(\mathbf{x})-f(\mathbf{v})\geq\alpha\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{v}\|,\ \forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}. (7) We note that polyhedral functions have been used for stochastic network optimization ( Huang and Neely, 2011 ) and geographical load balancing ( Lin et al., 2012 ) . Following Chen et al. (2018) , we set the switching cost as m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) = ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1})=\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\| . Intuitively, we may expect that the switching cost should be taken into consideration when making decisions. However, our analysis shows that minimizing the hitting cost alone yields the tightest competitive ratio so far. Specifically, we consider the following naive approach that ignores the switching cost and selects 𝐱 t = argmin 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 f t ​ ( 𝐱 ) . \mathbf{x}_{t}=\argmin_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}f_{t}(\mathbf{x}). (8) The theoretical guarantee of ( 8 ) is stated below. Theorem 1 . Suppose each f t ​ ( ⋅ ) : 𝒳 → ℝ + f_{t}(\cdot):\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} with minimizer 𝐯 t \mathbf{v}_{t} is α \alpha -polyhedral. We have ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ ) ≤ max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) ​ ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) + ‖ 𝐮 t − 𝐮 t − 1 ‖ ) \sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\|\big)\leq\max\left(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}\right)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})+\|\mathbf{u}_{t}-\mathbf{u}_{t-1}\|\big) (9) for every comparator sequence 𝐮 0 , 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X} with 𝐱 0 = 𝐮 0 \mathbf{x}_{0}=\mathbf{u}_{0} . Moreover, the above bound is tight for the naive algorithm, even on the one-dimensional domain 𝒳 = [ − 1 , 1 ] \mathcal{X}=[-1,1] . Remark: Our max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}) competitive ratio is much better than the 3 + 8 α 3+\frac{8}{\alpha} ratio of OBD ( Chen et al., 2018 ) , and also improves upon the 1 + 2 α 1+\frac{2}{\alpha} bound established by Lin et al. (2020) for ( 8 ). Furthermore, the proof of Theorem 1 is much simpler than that of OBD and refines the analysis of Lin et al. (2020, Lemma 1) . We next examine the effect of explicitly accounting for the switching cost through a fixed weight in the greedy algorithm ( 4 ). Proposition 1 . Fix α > 0 \alpha>0 . For any fixed γ ≥ 0 \gamma\geq 0 , the worst-case competitive ratio of the greedy algorithm ( 4 ), with the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, over nonnegative α \alpha -polyhedral hitting costs is at least max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max\left(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}\right) , regardless of how ties are broken. Moreover, when γ < α \gamma<\alpha , the algorithm coincides with the naive algorithm, whereas when γ > α \gamma>\alpha , its competitive ratio is unbounded. For α ≥ 2 \alpha\geq 2 , Theorem 1 gives a competitive ratio of 1 1 , which is optimal. For 1 ≤ α < 2 1\leq\alpha<2 , we establish a matching lower bound for deterministic online algorithms, yielding the following optimality result for all α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 . Theorem 2 . For α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 , the naive algorithm achieves the optimal competitive ratio max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max\left(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}\right) among deterministic online algorithms for nonnegative α \alpha -polyhedral hitting costs with the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost. Remark: For 0 < α < 1 0<\alpha<1 , the optimal deterministic competitive ratio remains open. Proposition 1 shows that any improvement over the naive guarantee would require going beyond the greedy algorithm with a fixed switching-cost weight.

sections.heading: 3.2 Quadratic Growth Functions
sections.text: In this section, we consider the quadratic growth condition. Definition 2 . A function f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) : 𝒳 → ℝ f(\cdot):\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} with minimizer 𝐯 \mathbf{v} is λ \lambda -quadratic growth if f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) − f ⁡ ( 𝐯 ) ≥ λ 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 − 𝐯 ‖ 2 , ∀ 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 . f(\mathbf{x})-f(\mathbf{v})\geq\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{v}\|^{2},\ \forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}. (10) The quadratic growth condition has been exploited by the optimization community ( Drusvyatskiy and Lewis, 2018 ; Necoara et al., 2019 ) to establish linear convergence, and this condition is weaker than strong convexity ( Hazan and Kale, 2011 ) . Following Goel et al. (2019) , we set the switching cost as m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) = ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ 2 / 2 m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1})=\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\|^{2}/2 . We also consider the naive approach in ( 8 ) and have the following theoretical guarantee. Theorem 3 . Suppose each f t ​ ( ⋅ ) : 𝒳 → ℝ + f_{t}(\cdot):\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} with minimizer 𝐯 t \mathbf{v}_{t} is λ \lambda -quadratic growth. We have ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ 2 ) ≤ ( 1 + 4 λ ) ​ ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) + 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐮 t − 𝐮 t − 1 ‖ 2 ) , \begin{split}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\|^{2}\right)\leq\left(1+\frac{4}{\lambda}\right)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{t}-\mathbf{u}_{t-1}\|^{2}\right),\end{split} for every comparator sequence 𝐮 0 , 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X} with 𝐱 0 = 𝐮 0 \mathbf{x}_{0}=\mathbf{u}_{0} . Remark: The above theorem implies that the naive approach achieves a competitive ratio of 1 + 4 λ 1+\frac{4}{\lambda} , which matches the order of the lower bound for this algorithm as λ \lambda tends to zero ( Goel et al., 2019 , Theorem 5) . Furthermore, it is also much better than the max ⁡ ( 1 + 6 λ , 4 ) \max(1+\frac{6}{\lambda},4) ratio established by Lin et al. (2020) for ( 8 ). Whether explicitly accounting for the switching cost can improve this guarantee under the quadratic growth condition alone remains open.

sections.text: When f t ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{t}(\cdot) is both quasiconvex and λ \lambda -quadratic growth, Goel et al. (11) The theoretical guarantee of ( 11 ) is stated below. Theorem 4 . Suppose the domain 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is convex, and each f t ​ ( ⋅ ) : 𝒳 → ℝ + f_{t}(\cdot):\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} with minimizer 𝐯 t \mathbf{v}_{t} is convex and λ \lambda -quadratic growth. By setting γ = λ λ + λ , \gamma=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\sqrt{\lambda}}, we have ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ 2 ) ≤ ( 1 + 2 λ ) ​ ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) + 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐮 t − 𝐮 t − 1 ‖ 2 ) , \sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\|^{2}\right)\leq\left(1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\right)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{t}-\mathbf{u}_{t-1}\|^{2}\right), (12) for every comparator sequence 𝐮 0 , 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X} with 𝐱 0 = 𝐮 0 \mathbf{x}_{0}=\mathbf{u}_{0} . Remark: Under the additional convexity assumption, accounting for switching costs improves the competitive-ratio bound from 1 + 4 λ 1+\frac{4}{\lambda} to 1 + 2 λ 1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}} when λ \lambda is small. According to the 1 2 + 1 2 ​ 1 + 4 λ \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{\lambda}} lower bound of the competitive ratio of strongly convex functions ( Goel et al., 2019 , Theorem 1) , the ratio in Theorem 4 is optimal up to constant factors. sections.text: When considering dynamic regret with switching cost, we adopt the common assumptions of online convex optimization (OCO) ( Shalev-Shwartz, 2011 ) . Assumption 1 . All functions f t f_{t} are convex over their domain 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . Assumption 2 . The domain 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is convex and has bounded diameter D D , i.e., max 𝐱 , 𝐱 ′ ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ ‖ 𝐱 − 𝐱 ′ ‖ ≤ D . \max_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|\leq D. sections.text: We first follow the standard setting of OCO in which the learner cannot observe the hitting cost when making predictions, and develop an algorithm based on Ader ( Zhang et al., 2018a ) , which is designed to minimize the dynamic regret w.r.t. any comparator sequence. Ader runs multiple OGD instances with different step sizes as expert-algorithms, and uses Hedge as the meta-algorithm to aggregate predictions from experts. In Ader, the meta-algorithm uses the hitting cost f t ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{t}(\cdot) or its linearized variant to measure the performance of experts. Specifically, we demonstrate that a small modification to Ader, which modifies the loss of the meta-algorithm to take into account the switching cost of experts, is sufficient to minimize the dynamic regret with switching cost. sections.heading: 4.2 The Lookahead Setting
sections.text: We next turn to the lookahead setting and investigate whether access to the current hitting cost can yield a stronger guarantee. We show that a lookahead version of SAder achieves a regret bound of the same order while removing Assumption 3 ; in particular, neither the gradients nor the hitting costs need to be bounded.

sections.heading: 5 Best of Both Worlds
sections.text: In the preceding sections, we have studied the competitive ratio and dynamic regret with switching cost separately. We now investigate whether a single algorithm can simultaneously achieve strong guarantees for both performance measures. We first consider the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost and then extend our approach to its squared counterpart.

sections.heading: 5.1 Technical Challenges
sections.text: For the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) = ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1})=\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\| , Daniely and Mansour (2019) developed a general framework for combining competitive-ratio and regret guarantees in the presence of switching costs. Following this principle, we consider two experts, designed respectively for competitive ratio and dynamic regret with switching cost, and aggregate their predictions using the Discounted-Normal-Predictor (DNP) ( Kapralov and Panigrahy, 2010 ; Kapralov and Panigrahy, 2011 ) . Even in the presence of switching costs, DNP guarantees constant regret w.r.t. the first expert and O ~ ​ ( T ) \widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}) regret w.r.t. the second expert. Consequently, the resulting meta-algorithm preserves the competitive-ratio guarantee of the former up to a constant additive term while adding only an O ~ ​ ( T ) \widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}) term to the dynamic-regret bound of the latter. Directly applying this methodology requires a known bound on the one-round cost difference between the two experts to normalize the feedback supplied to DNP. On a bounded domain, the bounded-gradient Assumption 3 would provide such a bound. However, the naive algorithm and lookahead SAder achieve their respective guarantees without assuming bounded gradients (Theorems 1 and 6 ). We therefore seek to aggregate these two experts without introducing this additional assumption. The lookahead protocol provides a way to overcome this difficulty: after observing the current hitting cost and obtaining the predictions of the two experts, the meta-algorithm knows their current cost difference before making its own decision. This additional information motivates a lookahead-aware variant of DNP that operates without a prescribed bound on the experts’ cost differences.

sections.text: We consider two arbitrary experts, denoted by E 0 E^{0} and E 1 E^{1} , and initialize both at a common point 𝐱 0 ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathcal{X} . sections.heading: 5.3 Squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -Norm Switching Cost
sections.text: We now consider the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) = 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ 2 . m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1})=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\|^{2}. We again consider two arbitrary experts, E 0 E^{0} and E 1 E^{1} , initialized at a common point 𝐱 0 ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathcal{X} . After observing f t ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{t}(\cdot) at round t t , the two experts produce candidate decisions 𝐱 t 0 \mathbf{x}_{t}^{0} and 𝐱 t 1 \mathbf{x}_{t}^{1} , respectively. Define the one-round cost of expert E i E^{i} by C t i = f t ​ ( 𝐱 t i ) + 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 t i − 𝐱 t − 1 i ‖ 2 , i ∈ { 0 , 1 } . C_{t}^{i}=f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{i})+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}_{t}^{i}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{i}\|^{2},\ i\in\{0,1\}. (34) Let Δ t = C t 0 − C t 1 \Delta_{t}=C_{t}^{0}-C_{t}^{1} denote their cost difference. sections.heading: 7 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: This paper establishes competitive-ratio and dynamic-regret guarantees for simple algorithms in smoothed online learning. The naive algorithm achieves strong competitive guarantees for polyhedral and quadratic growth hitting costs without requiring convexity. For polyhedral hitting costs, its guarantee is tight, and the algorithm is optimal among deterministic online algorithms for α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 . For convex quadratic growth hitting costs, the greedy algorithm improves upon the naive guarantee when the growth parameter is small. For general convex hitting costs, SAder and its lookahead counterpart achieve optimal dynamic regret in terms of the horizon and the comparator’s path-length. Lookahead removes the bounded-gradient assumption without improving the worst-case order of regret. UDNP complements these results by combining competitive-ratio and dynamic-regret guarantees under both the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm and squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching costs. Using lookahead information, it handles potentially unbounded expert-cost differences while controlling the additional switching cost of aggregation. Its guarantees apply to arbitrary pairs of experts, allowing improvements in either expert to be incorporated without redesigning the aggregation method. Several directions deserve further investigation. 1. A natural direction is to exploit polyhedrality or quadratic growth of convex hitting costs to sharpen dynamic-regret bounds under the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost and characterize their dependence on the comparator’s path-length and the growth parameters. 2. For α \alpha -polyhedral hitting costs with 0 < α < 1 0<\alpha<1 , the optimal deterministic competitive ratio remains open. For quadratic growth hitting costs without convexity, it remains open whether accounting for switching costs can improve the naive guarantee. Sharper lower bounds would help characterize the optimal competitive ratios in these settings.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.24370v1 [cs.LG] 17 Oct 2026 Lijun Zhang, Linzhe He, Wei Jiang, and Shiyin Lu Revisiting Smoothed Online Learning: Competitive Ratio, Dynamic Regret with Switching Cost, and Best of Both Worlds Lijun Zhang zhanglj@lamda.nju.edu.cn Affiliation: Linzhe He helz@lamda.nju.edu.cn Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210023, China School of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210023, China Wei Jiang 12025220@njust.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing 210094, China Shiyin Lu running.lsy@alibaba-inc.com Affiliation: Alibaba Group, Hangzhou 310052, China Abstract We revisit smoothed online learning and develop algorithms with improved competitive ratios, optimal dynamic regret with switching cost, and best-of-both-worlds guarantees. Surprisingly, minimizing the hitting cost alone is max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}) -competitive for α \alpha -polyhedral functions under the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost and 1 + 4 λ 1+\frac{4}{\lambda} -competitive for λ \lambda -quadratic growth functions under the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, significantly improving existing guarantees. The polyhedral bound is tight for this naive algorithm, and we establish a matching lower bound for α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 . For convex λ \lambda -quadratic growth hitting costs, minimizing a suitably weighted sum of hitting and squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching costs yields a competitive ratio of 1 + 2 λ 1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}} . For dynamic regret with the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, we develop Smoothed Ader (SAder), which achieves the optimal O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) rate in the standard online convex optimization setting, where P T P_{T} is the comparator’s path-length. Its lookahead version removes the bounded-gradient assumption, and a matching lower bound establishes optimality in this setting. Finally, for convex hitting costs on a bounded convex domain, we develop UDNP to aggregate any two experts in the lookahead setting under both switching costs. Its additional cumulative cost is at most O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) relative to the first expert and O ⁡ ( T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(\sqrt{T\log T}) relative to the second, yielding best-of-both-worlds guarantees without bounded gradients. † † heading: 23 2022 1- 1/21; Revised 5/22 9/22 21-0000 † † shortheadings: Revisiting Smoothed Online Learning / Zhang, He, Jiang, and Lu † † firstpage: 1 † † editor: My editor keywords Smoothed online learning, Online convex optimization, Competitive ratio, Dynamic regret with switching cost, Best of both worlds 1 Introduction Online learning is the process of making a sequence of predictions given knowledge of the answers to previous tasks and possibly additional information ( Shalev-Shwartz, 2011 ) . While traditional online learning aims to make the prediction as accurate as possible, in this paper, we study smoothed online learning (SOL), where the online learner incurs a switching cost for changing its predictions between rounds ( Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2013 ) . SOL has received considerable attention recently because in many real-world applications, a change of action usually brings some additional cost. Examples include the dynamic right-sizing for data centers ( Lin et al., 2011 ) , geographical load balancing ( Lin et al., 2012 ) , real-time electricity pricing ( Kim and Giannakis, 2014 ) , video streaming ( Joseph and de Veciana, 2012 ) , spatiotemporal sequence prediction ( Kim et al., 2015 ) , multi-timescale control ( Goel et al., 2017 ) , and thermal management ( Zanini et al., 2010 ) . Specifically, SOL is performed in a sequence of consecutive rounds, where at round t t the learner is asked to select a point 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} from the decision set 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , and suffers a hitting cost f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) . Depending on the performance metric, the learner may be allowed to observe f t ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{t}(\cdot) when making decisions, which is different from the traditional online learning in which f t ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{t}(\cdot) is revealed only after the learner submits its decision ( Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2006 ) . Additionally, the learner also incurs a switching cost m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1}) for changing decisions between successive rounds. Common choices for the switching cost include the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm distance ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ \|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\| and the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 t − 1 ‖ 2 / 2 \|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\|^{2}/2 ( Goel et al., 2019 ) . In the literature, there are two performance metrics for SOL: competitive ratio and dynamic regret with switching cost. Competitive ratio is popular in the community of online algorithms ( Borodin and El-Yaniv, 1998 ) . It is defined as the worst-case ratio of the total cost incurred by the online learner to the offline optimal cost: ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) ) min ⁡ ∑ t = 1 T 𝐮 0 , 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ ( f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) + m ⁡ ( 𝐮 t , 𝐮 t − 1 ) ) . \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1})\big)}{\min_{\mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})+m(\mathbf{u}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t-1})\big)}. (1) When focusing on the competitive ratio, we consider the lookahead setting, in which the learner observes f t ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{t}(\cdot) before picking 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} . The problem is still nontrivial due to the coupling created by the switching cost. Dynamic regret with switching cost extends dynamic regret ( Zinkevich, 2003 ) by accounting for switching costs. Whereas competitive ratio measures a multiplicative comparison with the offline optimum, dynamic regret measures the additive difference between the learner’s total cost and that of an arbitrary comparator sequence 𝐮 0 , 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{u}_{0},\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X} : ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + m ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 t − 1 ) ) − ∑ t = 1 T ( f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) + m ⁡ ( 𝐮 t , 𝐮 t − 1 ) ) . \sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+m(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t-1})\big)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})+m(\mathbf{u}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t-1})\big). (2) We keep the comparator sequence explicit in ( 2 ), rather than minimizing over it as in previous work ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Goel et al., 2019 ) , and seek bounds that adapt to its regularity, measured by the path-length P T = ∑ t = 1 T ‖ 𝐮 t − 𝐮 t − 1 ‖ . P_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\mathbf{u}_{t}-\mathbf{u}_{t-1}\|. (3) For dynamic regret with switching cost, we consider both the standard OCO setting and the lookahead setting. Motivation Online balanced descent (OBD) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) balances the hitting and switching costs by projecting the previous decision onto a suitably chosen sublevel set of the current hitting-cost function. OBD and its variants ( Goel et al., 2019 ) exploit structural properties of the hitting costs to obtain dimension-free competitive ratios. These results motivate examining the simpler greedy algorithm, which selects its decision by solving min 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 f t ​ ( 𝐱 ) + γ ​ m ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐱 t − 1 ) , \min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\quad f_{t}(\mathbf{x})+\gamma m(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{t-1}), (4) where γ ≥ 0 \gamma\geq 0 is a trade-off parameter. As a special case of Regularized OBD (R-OBD), a suitably tuned greedy algorithm achieves the optimal competitive ratio for strongly convex hitting costs under the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost ( Goel et al., 2019 ) . Moreover, Lin et al. (2020) analyze the choice γ = 0 \gamma=0 , referred to as the naive approach, for polyhedral and quadratic growth functions. We revisit these simple algorithms to sharpen their competitive guarantees under different growth conditions and to clarify when explicitly accounting for switching costs improves performance. For dynamic regret, neither the guarantee of OBD nor that of R-OBD provides an adaptive bound for the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost. OBD requires a prescribed upper bound on the comparator’s path-length, and its regret bound depends on this upper bound rather than the actual path-length ( Chen et al., 2018 , Corollary 11) . R-OBD provides an adaptive guarantee, but for the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost ( Goel et al., 2019 ) . Moreover, both guarantees require lookahead access to the current hitting cost. We therefore seek adaptive dynamic-regret guarantees for the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost under both standard and lookahead feedback. We also investigate whether a single algorithm can achieve both a competitive-ratio guarantee and an adaptive dynamic-regret guarantee, connecting to earlier work on combining the two criteria ( Andrew et al., 2013 ; Daniely and Mansour, 2019 ) . Expert aggregation offers a natural approach, but directly applying this approach requires a known bound on the experts’ one-round cost differences. We investigate how lookahead information can overcome this obstacle without imposing an additional bounded-gradient assumption. Our contributions are summarized as follows. Competitive Ratio We sharpen the competitive guarantees of the naive and greedy algorithms and establish complementary lower bounds. For α \alpha -polyhedral hitting costs and the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, the naive algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max\left(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}\right) . This improves upon the 3 + 8 α 3+\frac{8}{\alpha} ratio of OBD ( Chen et al., 2018 ) and the 1 + 2 α 1+\frac{2}{\alpha} bound of Lin et al. (2020, Lemma 1) . We show that this bound is tight for the naive algorithm and cannot be improved by any fixed choice of γ \gamma in the greedy algorithm. Moreover, we establish a matching lower bound for α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 . For λ \lambda -quadratic growth hitting costs and the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, the naive algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of 1 + 4 λ 1+\frac{4}{\lambda} , improving upon the max ⁡ ( 1 + 6 λ , 4 ) \max\left(1+\frac{6}{\lambda},4\right) bound of Lin et al. (2020, Lemma 1) and matching, as λ \lambda tends to zero, the order of the lower bound for this algorithm in Goel et al. (2019, Theorem 5) . Neither this guarantee nor the polyhedral guarantee requires convexity. Under additional convexity, a suitable choice of γ > 0 \gamma>0 yields a competitive ratio of 1 + 2 λ 1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}} , improving the naive guarantee for small λ \lambda . Compared with Greedy OBD ( Goel et al., 2019 , Theorem 3) , our guarantee has the same asymptotic order with much smaller constants, although it requires convexity rather than quasiconvexity. Our analysis of the naive and greedy algorithms is also simpler, avoiding the geometric arguments used for OBD and Greedy OBD. Dynamic Regret with Switching Cost For convex hitting costs and the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, we develop Smoothed Ader (SAder) by extending Ader ( Zhang et al., 2018a ) , an algorithm that achieves optimal dynamic regret in standard online convex optimization. Ader uses Hedge ( Freund and Schapire, 1997 ) to aggregate online gradient descent (OGD) experts ( Zinkevich, 2003 ) with different step sizes. SAder modifies this approach by incorporating the experts’ switching costs into the meta-algorithm’s losses. Under the standard bounded-domain and bounded-gradient assumptions, SAder achieves an optimal O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) bound on the sum of dynamic regret and the learner’s switching cost, matching Ader’s rate despite the additional switching cost. Compared with OBD ( Chen et al., 2018 , Corollary 11) , SAder adapts to the actual path-length P T P_{T} without requiring a prescribed upper bound on P T P_{T} or lookahead feedback. We further develop lookahead SAder, whose greedy experts generate predictions using the current hitting cost. The meta-algorithm updates the aggregation weights using the experts’ current one-round costs before making its decision. Lookahead SAder achieves the same O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) regret bound without assuming bounded gradients. We establish a matching Ω ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) \Omega(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) lower bound in the lookahead setting, showing that this rate is optimal up to constant factors. Best of Both Worlds We develop UDNP, an unbounded-input variant of the Discounted-Normal-Predictor ( Kapralov and Panigrahy, 2011 ) , to aggregate any two experts in the lookahead setting. Building on expert aggregation with switching costs ( Daniely and Mansour, 2019 ) , UDNP exploits lookahead information to handle potentially unbounded differences between the experts’ one-round costs, without requiring a prescribed bound on these differences or a bounded-gradient assumption. Our approach applies to both the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm and squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching costs. For convex hitting costs on a bounded convex domain, the learner’s total cost exceeds that of the first expert by at most a constant and that of the second expert by at most O ⁡ ( T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(\sqrt{T\log T}) . Thus, when the first expert provides a competitive-ratio guarantee and the second a dynamic-regret guarantee, UDNP preserves the former up to an additive constant while adding only an O ⁡ ( T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(\sqrt{T\log T}) term to the latter. As concrete applications, we instantiate this approach with experts analyzed in this paper. For convex hitting costs satisfying the α \alpha -polyhedral condition, combining the naive algorithm with lookahead SAder under the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost yields the competitive factor max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max\left(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}\right) up to an additive constant and an O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) + T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}+\sqrt{T\log T}) dynamic-regret bound. For convex hitting costs satisfying the λ \lambda -quadratic growth condition, combining two greedy experts under the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost yields the competitive factor 1 + 2 λ 1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}} up to an additive constant and an O ⁡ ( P T + T ​ log ⁡ T ) O(P_{T}+\sqrt{T\log T}) dynamic-regret bound. Extensions over the Conference Version A preliminary version of this paper was presented at the 35th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) . The present paper extends that version in the following aspects: • We extend the competitive-ratio analysis for polyhedral hitting costs. We prove that the max ⁡ ( 1 , 2 α ) \max\left(1,\frac{2}{\alpha}\right) bound from the conference version is tight for the naive algorithm and cannot be improved by any fixed choice of γ \gamma in the greedy algorithm. We further establish a matching lower bound for α ≥ 1 \alpha\geq 1 . • We develop UDNP to address the best-of-both-worlds question left open in the conference version. For the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost, we establish general guarantees for aggregating arbitrary pairs of experts while handling potentially unbounded cost differences without assuming bounded gradients. We instantiate these guarantees by combining the naive algorithm with lookahead SAder. • We extend UDNP to the squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching cost through a new interpolation inequality. The resulting aggregation guarantee also applies to arbitrary pairs of experts, and we instantiate it with two greedy experts. We further establish a dynamic-regret bound for the greedy algorithm under general convexity, allowing nonsmooth hitting costs and constrained minimizers. • We revise lookahead SAder to update its aggregation weights using the experts’ current one-round costs, removing the circular dependence on the current meta-decision. We also provide a proof based on the strong convexity of the experts’ regularized objectives, without requiring differentiability of the hitting costs. Organization We review related work in Section 2 and study the competitive ratios of the naive and greedy algorithms in Section 3 . Section 4 develops SAder and its lookahead variant for dynamic regret with switching cost. The best-of-both-worlds framework, UDNP, is presented in Section 5 for both the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm and squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching costs. Proofs of the main results appear in Section 6 , with proofs of supporting lemmas deferred to the appendices. We conclude the paper and discuss future directions in Section 7 . 2 Related Work This section reviews related work on smoothed online learning (SOL), dynamic regret, and online optimization with switching constraints. 2.1 Smoothed Online Learning SOL has been investigated under the setting of multi-armed bandits ( Agrawal et al., 1990 ; Guha and Munagala, 2009 ; Dekel et al., 2014 ; Koren et al., 2017a ; Koren et al., 2017b ) , prediction with expert advice ( Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2013 ) , and online convex optimization ( Lin et al., 2011 ; Bansal et al., 2015 ; Zhao et al., 2020b ) . In the following, we mainly discuss smoothed online convex optimization (SOCO). The early works on SOCO are motivated by real-world applications with switching costs, and focus on designing competitive algorithms in the low-dimensional setting ( Lin et al., 2011 ) . In particular, Bansal et al. (2015) show that for SOCO on the real line, the competitive ratio can be upper bounded by 2 2 , which is proved to be optimal ( Antoniadis and Schewior, 2018 ) . They also establish a competitive ratio of 3 3 under the memoryless setting. In the study of SOCO, it is common to assume that the learner has access to predictions of future hitting costs, and several algorithms ( Lin et al., 2012 ; Chen et al., 2015 ; Chen et al., 2016 ; Li et al., 2018 ; Li and Li, 2020 ) have been developed based on receding horizon control (RHC) ( Kwon and Han, 2005 ) . In fact, the greedy algorithm in ( 4 ) can be treated as a variant of RHC. However, previous results for RHC are limited to special problems, and ( 4 ) remains under-explored. For example, with a prediction window of length W W , Li et al. (2018) derive a dynamic-regret bound with switching cost that decreases exponentially with W W , under assumptions including strong convexity and smoothness. One milestone is the online balanced descent (OBD) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) , which has a dimension-free competitive ratio even when the learner can only observe the hitting cost of the current round. Specifically, OBD iteratively projects the previous point onto a carefully chosen level set of the hitting cost so as to balance the switching cost and the hitting cost. When the hitting cost is α \alpha -polyhedral and convex, and the switching cost is the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm distance, OBD attains a 3 + 8 α 3+\frac{8}{\alpha} competitive ratio. Furthermore, OBD can also be tuned to control the dynamic regret with switching cost. Let L L be an upper bound of the path-length of the comparator sequence, i.e., P T ≤ L P_{T}\leq L . Chen et al. SOCO is closely related to convex body chasing (CBC), where the learner selects a point from each arriving convex body and seeks to minimize the total movement ( Friedman and Linial, 1993 ; Antoniadis et al., 2016 ; Bansal et al., 2018 ; Argue et al., 2019 ; Bubeck et al., 2019 ; Bubeck et al., 2020 ) . For general CBC in Euclidean space, algorithms achieve a competitive ratio of O ⁡ ( min ⁡ { d , d ​ log ⁡ T } ) O(\min\{d,\sqrt{d\log T}\}) ( Argue et al., 2020b ; Sellke, 2020 ) , while a lower bound of Ω ⁡ ( d ) \Omega(\sqrt{d}) is known ( Friedman and Linial, 1993 ) . Recent work investigates how to incorporate advice into competitive algorithms for SOCO and related chasing problems while retaining worst-case guarantees. Christianson et al. (2022) combine black-box advice with a competitive algorithm for convex body and function chasing; for polyhedral hitting costs, they use the naive approach from our conference version ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) as the competitive baseline. For possibly nonconvex α \alpha -polyhedral hitting costs, Rutten et al. (2023) establish near-optimal tradeoffs between consistency and robustness with untrusted predictions. Christianson et al. (2023) further characterize such tradeoffs in the more general framework of metrical task systems. Recent work also develops dynamic-regret guarantees for SOCO in several directions. Zhang et al. (2022) obtain interval-wise regret guarantees using Discounted-Normal-Predictor ( Kapralov and Panigrahy, 2011 ) , while Yang et al. (2025) consider delayed gradient feedback. Mhaisen and Iosifidis (2026) introduce partially lazy gradient updates and aggregate the resulting experts using the SAder meta-algorithm from our conference version ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) , retaining the optimal O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) dynamic regret with switching cost. Alongside these dynamic-regret results, Bhuyan et al. (2024) seek simultaneous guarantees in adversarial and stochastic environments. For quadratic hitting costs and squared ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm switching costs, they combine adversarial competitiveness with near-optimal stochastic performance when the hitting-cost minimizers form a martingale whose increments have a common covariance matrix. Our focus is on simultaneously controlling the competitive ratio and dynamic regret against arbitrary comparator sequences in the lookahead setting. The motivation of dynamic regret is to deal with changing environments, in which the optimal decision may change over time. It is defined as the difference between the cumulative loss of the learner and that of a sequence of comparators 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X} : D-Regret ( 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T ) = ∑ t = 1 T f t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) − ∑ t = 1 T f t ​ ( 𝐮 t ) . \DReg(\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t}). (6) In the general form of dynamic regret, 𝐮 1 , … , 𝐮 T \mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T} could be an arbitrary sequence ( Zinkevich, 2003 ; Hall and Willett, 2013 ; Zhang et al., 2018a ; Zhang et al., 2020 ; Cutkosky, 2020 ; Zhao et al., 2020a ; Baby and Wang, 2021 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . In the restricted form, the comparators are chosen as per-round minimizers, i.e., 𝐮 t ∈ argmin 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 f t ​ ( 𝐱 ) \mathbf{u}_{t}\in\argmin_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}f_{t}(\mathbf{x}) ( Jadbabaie et al., 2015 ; Besbes et al., 2015 ; Yang et al., 2016 ; Mokhtari et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ; Zhang et al., 2018b ; Wan et al., 2021 ; Zhao and Zhang, 2021 ; Xu and Zhang, 2024 ) . While it is well-known that sublinear dynamic regret is unattainable in the worst case, one can bound the dynamic regret in terms of some regularities of the comparator sequence. An instance is given by Zinkevich (2003) , who introduces the notion of path-length defined in ( 3 ) to measure the temporal variability of the comparator sequence, and derives an O ​ ( T ​ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T}(1+P_{T})) bound for the dynamic regret of OGD. Later, Zhang et al. (2018a) develop adaptive learning for dynamic environment (Ader), which achieves the optimal O ⁡ ( T ⁡ ( 1 + P T ) ) O(\sqrt{T(1+P_{T})}) dynamic regret. In this paper, we show that a small change of Ader attains the same bound for dynamic regret with switching cost. Chen et al. (2020) characterize the minimax regret when the learner is allowed only a limited number of switches. Sherman and Koren (2023) study a related formulation in which the switching budget is imposed in expectation. Subsequent work improves regret guarantees under this expected switch-count budget ( Agarwal et al., 2023 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , with Agarwal et al. (2024) obtaining better dimension dependence without requiring smooth losses. Beyond switch-count constraints, Wang et al. (2021) impose a budget on the cumulative movement of the learner and establish minimax-optimal regret bounds for convex losses. This formulation accounts for the distance between consecutive decisions, allowing finer control over movement than counting each change equally. These studies minimize hitting-cost regret against the best fixed decision while satisfying a prescribed switching budget. In our setting, switching costs are included in the objective together with hitting costs, so the learner directly trades off the two types of costs. 3 Competitive Ratio In this section, we study competitive ratio as the performance metric.
